format.label: A memo to a CMO
format.instruction: Write it as a short internal memo to a chief marketing officer. Plain language, no jargon they would have to look up. Around 120 words.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Memo to the CMO

I don't think we should try to build one brain that picks the best message everywhere. That's the obvious answer and I think it fails: the data is too late, the channels too uneven, and nobody agrees what "best" means.

Instead I'd start by preventing harm, not chasing optimal. One shared record of what we've said to a person and what we promised them, plus a small set of rules every channel must obey: contact limits, one live offer per person, service always outranks selling. Rules are enforceable even when data is stale.

Then we earn the right to optimize: pick two channels with real feedback, agree one number that counts value over months rather than days, and test against holdouts.

The hard part is budgets. If channel owners are paid on their own numbers, they'll route around any shared layer. I'd want your air cover on that before I spend engineering money.
answers.first_move: Build one shared log of every message and promise we've made to each customer, readable by all channels.
answers.hardest_part: There is no agreed definition of a good outcome, so "optimal" is undefined before the technology is even the issue.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
To: CMO

Subject: Where to start on cross-channel orchestration

I would not begin with an AI “brain” controlling every channel. The data, incentives and feedback are not reliable enough.

Start with two high-volume journeys across three channels where collisions are visible. Create shared rules for eligibility, contact limits, offer consistency and service exceptions. Log every decision, exposure, cost and outcome, then use customer-level control groups to measure incremental value over months, not clicks over days.

Initially, the central layer should constrain harmful actions and recommend priorities; channel teams can retain execution. Expand its authority only when tests show gains in margin, retention or service without increasing fatigue.

The main work is organizational: one scorecard, explicit trade-offs, and budget rules that prevent channels from claiming the same result. Even then, incomplete identity and delayed outcomes will limit optimization.
answers.first_move: I would first choose two journeys where conflicting messages are common and financially measurable.
answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is agreeing who can sacrifice a channel’s short-term results for a better overall customer outcome.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: Vendors pitch a single central brain that orchestrates every touchpoint, but chasing that is a trap. If we try to algorithmically plan complete customer journeys across every tool, latency, broken data, and channel politics will break it immediately. Instead of building a master conductor, we should build a negative filter: an arbitration layer that only handles constraints. We let email, ads, and web teams run their own engines, but we give a shared system the absolute authority to block conflicting offers, enforce quiet periods, and cap overall contact fatigue. We will quickly run into resistance because channel heads will lose immediate clicks, and proving long-term retention gains takes months. But coordinating by restraint is the only practical starting point.
answers.first_move: Implement a shared frequency cap across email and push that stops teams from messaging the same person twice in twenty-four hours.
answers.hardest_part: Getting channel owners to accept lower short-term metrics when the system silences them for the broader customer experience.

format.label: Three moves
format.instruction: Give exactly three moves, in order. One sentence each, then one sentence on what makes that move hard. Nothing else.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach: Move 1: Instead of building the single decision brain everyone proposes, build a global veto — a contact-rights and offer-consistency ledger that every channel must check before send, which arbitrates (suppress, defer, downgrade) but never decides what to send. Hard part: the ledger only works if the slowest, dumbest execution systems honor it, and ad platforms and batch ESPs give you a check window measured in hours or days, so you're writing policy against stale state and have to decide which channels get a hard gate versus a probabilistic one. Move 2: Establish a person-level global holdout — a population suppressed or lightly treated across every channel simultaneously — and make it the only sanctioned way to claim incremental value, so the objective function gets discovered empirically instead of negotiated in a committee. Hard part: it costs real revenue, leaks constantly through unsuppressible surfaces like organic search and service contacts, and the long-term-value half of the answer doesn't resolve for two to four quarters, which is longer than most sponsors' patience or tenure. Move 3: Convert the veto into an internal market — channels keep their budgets and their own KPIs but bid for a finite number of contact slots per person per window at a shadow price derived from the holdout-measured fatigue cost, so coordination happens through price rather than through org redesign. Hard part: you need an exchange rate between a service deflection, a margin dollar and a churn-risk point that finance will defend, and any bidding system with internally-forecast values gets gamed within a quarter unless bids settle against measured outcomes.
answers.first_move: Stand up a shared pre-send check that any channel must call, and start by using it only to suppress and deduplicate, not to choose messages.
answers.hardest_part: There is no measurable global objective until you pay for a cross-channel holdout, and the signal that matters most — long-term value — arrives far too late to steer a real-time decision.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
Move 1: Reject the obvious “single global brain” starting point and define a measurable portfolio objective for a few high-conflict journeys, with explicit weights for margin, fatigue, service cost, customer harm, and long-term value plus persistent holdouts.
What makes this move hard: The weights are business and governance choices rather than modeling facts, and channel owners will resist measurements that expose local gains as globally harmful.
Move 2: Build a thin coordination layer that maintains shared customer state and issues only enforceable decisions such as eligibility, suppression, contact budgets, offer consistency, and channel priority while existing platforms retain execution.
What makes this move hard: Identity gaps, stale signals, uneven APIs, and platforms that acknowledge instructions without reliably applying them make the decision layer’s actual control uncertain.
Move 3: Start in shadow mode, estimate incremental cross-channel effects with randomized exploration where safe, and gradually delegate bounded decisions to constrained learning policies with hard customer, legal, and commercial guardrails.
What makes this move hard: Outcomes are delayed, confounded, sparse, and nonstationary, so proving that a policy improves the whole journey rather than reallocating credit is genuinely difficult.
answers.first_move: Choose a few conflicting journeys and agree on how success and customer harm will be measured.
answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is creating an objective and control structure that channel owners will accept despite conflicting incentives and unreliable feedback.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: 1. Strip decision logic out of the channel tools and turn them into dumb execution endpoints that only fire when granted a centralized token. What makes this hard is that channel teams and vendors fiercely resist losing autonomy, and native platform features actively work against it. 2. Model customer fatigue and negative cross-channel interference first, rather than trying to predict optimal positive actions. What makes this hard is that attributing delayed customer burnout across fragmented identifiers is statistically messy and directly contradicts short-term campaign goals. 3. Replace channel-specific ROI attribution with an internal tax on downstream friction to force budget owners toward shared constraints. What makes this hard is that resolving conflicting executive incentives requires political will that no software architecture can engineer on its own.
answers.first_move: I would stop letting individual channel tools decide when to send messages.
answers.hardest_part: You cannot mathematically optimize a shared experience when the humans running the channels are measured on conflicting quarterly goals.

format.label: Pseudocode
format.instruction: Express the approach as short annotated pseudocode. The comments should carry the reasoning; the code should carry the structure. Around 15 lines.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
```
# Premise I'd push back on: do NOT build the global optimizer first.
# Nobody will hand a new layer the right to *send*. They will hand it the right to *stop*.
# Negative control is politically cheap and captures most of the harm.

loop every_event:
  state = union(channel_states)            # accept it's stale+partial; attach age+confidence,
                                           # and make staleness a first-class input, not a bug to fix later
  bids = [ch.propose(state) for ch in channels]   # channels keep their own models. Rebuilding them is a 3-year detour.

  for b in bids:
    b.value = calibrate(b.stated_value, ch.history)  # channels WILL inflate bids. Score them on realized
                                                     # incremental margin, not claimed. Liars get discounted.

  # the missing objective function: don't convene a committee to agree one.
  # Fix ONE scarce resource (customer attention) and let price discovery do the rest.
  shadow_price = fatigue_price(customer, from=contact_holdout)  # learned, person-level, nonstationary
  decision = allow(b) if b.value > shadow_price + contradiction_penalty(b, recent_promises)
             else suppress_or_delay(b)

  emit(decision)                           # veto/defer only. Channel still executes. No budget is seized.
  log(decision, counterfactual_arm)

# measurement is the whole game:
maintain GLOBAL_HOLDOUT at customer level, 12+ month horizon, never touched by the arbiter
  # message-level tests cannot see journey-level harm; that's why the industry keeps missing this
# only after the holdout proves the veto layer pays, bid for positive control of one adjacent pair of channels
```
What I expect to go wrong: the shadow price of contact is person-specific, nonstationary, and confounded with intent, so early fatigue models will mostly rediscover "people about to churn stop opening email." Contradiction detection is harder than fatigue because it needs a semantic model of what was promised, and offer metadata across platforms is garbage. And the holdout will be raided within two quarters by someone who needs the revenue.
answers.first_move: Build a veto-only arbitration layer that can stop or delay messages but never send them, and put a long-horizon customer-level holdout behind it.
answers.hardest_part: There is no observable counterfactual for a whole journey at the individual level, so the price of contacting someone — the one number the whole system turns on — has to be inferred from deliberately withheld experience that the business is constantly incentivized to stop withholding.

# 1. Discard the fantasy of a central real-time decision brain; channels won't surrender execution or latency budgets.
# 2. Treat cross-channel coordination as an asynchronous scarcity problem (attention budget), not an optimization math problem.
def handle_touchpoint_request(customer_id, requesting_channel, proposed_action):
    # Reconstruct whatever state exists; accept that it is inherently stale and incomplete
    user_state = get_shared_state_view(customer_id) 
    
    # Compute the dynamic cost to interrupt based on recent cross-channel touches and service friction
    interruption_tax = compute_shadow_price(user_state.touch_history, user_state.active_support_tickets)
    
    # Obvious trap: trying to maximize global LTV. Realistically: just suppress negative externalities.
    net_benefit = proposed_action.expected_margin - proposed_action.cost - interruption_tax
    
    if net_benefit <= 0:
        # Log rejection as a counterfactual for attribution debates; do not fire
        return withhold_and_log(reason='negative_external_drag', candidate=proposed_action)
        
    # Reserve cooldown across all channels rather than dictating what they do
    acquire_distributed_lock(customer_id, duration=decay_window(proposed_action))
    return emit_execution_grant(proposed_action)

format.label: A checklist
format.instruction: Give a checklist someone could actually run next quarter. Each item concrete enough to be marked done or not done. Six items at most.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Up front, two disagreements with the standard answer.

First, I don't think you should start by trying to agree on an objective function. You won't get it, and chasing it burns the quarter in committee. The achievable version is a *constrained arbitration* problem: a set of hard constraints everyone already agrees on (don't upsell someone with an open P1 ticket, don't exceed N touches/week, don't contradict a live offer) plus one shared exchange rate for customer attention. One scalar price, not one utility function. That's a negotiation you can actually win.

Second, don't try to own execution. Every attempt at a central brain that *commands* channels dies on org politics. A layer with veto authority is politically cheap — channel owners keep their stacks, their budgets, their roadmaps — and veto gets you most of the value, because the big losses are contradiction and over-contact, not suboptimal selection. Positive coordination (orchestrating the right sequence) comes later, if ever. Be honest that "globally optimal" is not on the table; Pareto-improving coordination is.

The checklist:

1. **Unified exposure log.** One event schema, one identity key, every outbound touch and inbound service/commerce event appended within minutes. Done = published per-channel coverage report, with a hard number for what fraction of real touches land in the log and at what latency. Expect paid media to be hours-delayed and partially unattributable at the person level; write that down rather than papering over it.

2. **Conflict audit, in dollars.** Read-only analysis of the log: contradictory concurrent offers, contacts during open tickets, customers above fatigue thresholds, discount given to someone already converting. Done = a number you'd defend to a CFO, broken out by channel pair. This is both the scoping exercise and the political ammunition; without it you're asking people to give up autonomy on a hunch.

3. **Veto-only arbitration service, live in the two highest-volume channels.** Synchronous call, hard constraints only, <50ms p99, fail-open with the default decision logged. No optimization, no model. Done = it's in the send path and has actually blocked traffic. Fail-open is non-negotiable; the first time this thing takes down the web experience you lose the mandate.

4. **One exchange rate, signed.** Get agreement on a single scalar for expected contribution over a fixed short window (14 or 30 days), and a per-customer attention budget priced in it. Not a utility function — a price. Done = a one-page document with the formula, signed by the owners of email, app, web, paid and service. Expect the fight to be about whose conversions get discounted, not about the math.

5. **Customer-level global holdout with a pre-signed measurement contract.** 5–10% held out of arbitration entirely, reported at company level, with the restatement rule for channel-owner scorecards agreed *before* launch. Done = finance/analytics has signed it. Channel owners will resist because coordination taxes their reported numbers; if you haven't pre-negotiated how their targets move, the holdout result won't matter.

6. **Settlement rule for suppressed sends.** Written policy on how a channel is credited when it was vetoed and the customer converted elsewhere. Done = signed. This is the item everyone skips and it's the one that determines whether the layer survives its second quarter.

What I expect to run into: identity coverage on anonymous web traffic will be worse than anyone claims, and the arbitration layer will be making decisions about a partial customer. Paid platforms will not honour realtime suppression — their bidders will re-target people you excluded, so treat paid as weather, not a channel you control; you influence the distribution, not the event. The exchange rate will get gamed within a quarter of being published. And the short-horizon proxy will drift from long-term value in ways you can only detect with a holdout you keep running for a year, which is far longer than anyone's patience.
answers.first_move: Build the single log of every message we send and every service event, and publish how much of reality it actually captures per channel.
answers.hardest_part: There is no agreed way to price one channel's conversion against another's fatigue cost or service outcome, and the people who would have to agree are each measured on numbers that coordination makes worse.

- [ ] **Run a rules-based arbitration layer in shadow mode:** encode eligibility, frequency caps, conflicting-offer rules, budget constraints, fallback behavior, and channel precedence; compare its recommendations with actual channel actions for at least four weeks and quantify conflicts, prevented contacts, API failures, and stale-state decisions. Do not start with reinforcement learning—the causal signal and control surface are not ready.

format.label: Fifty words
format.instruction: Fifty words or fewer. No preamble, no caveats. The compression is the point: keep only what you would keep if you could keep one thing.

format.label: A lullaby
format.instruction: Write it as a short lullaby: three or four gentle rhyming couplets someone could actually sing. Soft on the surface, honest underneath. The problem is still unsolved when the song ends, and the song should know it.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Hush now, the channels all whisper at once,
six little bidders, each sure it's the one.
I'd not build the brain first — I'd build the gate:
one ledger of contact, one shared sense of state.

Not a model to rule them, a budget to spend,
fatigue as a currency, lent out and then lent again;
each channel may bid what a touch's truly worth,
and pay for the quiet it takes from the earth.

The feedback comes slow and the ad servers lie,
so hold out a holdout, and watch it, and sigh —
long-term value is a guess in a coat,
and the org chart, not math, is what sinks the boat.

Sleep, little stack, we'll not solve this tonight;
the objective's a treaty no one yet will write.
But a shared contact ledger is a thing we can keep —
and that's half the fight, love. Now go on to sleep.
